0.title: Christ Is All: Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
0.overview:
Colossians is the most christologically concentrated letter in the Pauline corpus. Its central argument can be stated in five words: Christ is all you need. The church at Colossae was being seduced by a sophisticated religious system — a blend of Jewish legal observance, angel veneration, ascetic practices, and esoteric philosophy that scholars call the “Colossian heresy.” The false teachers were not asking the Colossians to abandon Christ; they were proposing to supplement him, to add the fullness they implied Christ alone could not provide. Paul’s response is the great Christ hymn of chapter 1 and the devastating theological logic of chapter 2: in Christ “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him” (2:9–10). There is nothing to add. He is enough.

Paul wrote the letter from prison, most likely in Rome, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon — the so-called “Prison Epistles.” The church at Colossae had apparently been founded not by Paul himself but by Epaphras (1:7), one of Paul’s co-workers, during Paul’s extended ministry in Ephesus (Acts 19). Paul had never visited the church personally (2:1), and yet he writes with the pastoral urgency of a father: he is “struggling” for them (2:1), praying that they would have “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” hidden in Christ (2:3), warning them against the plausible-sounding deception that threatens to take them captive (2:8).

The letter’s structure is elegant. Chapters 1–2 are theological: the supremacy of Christ over all creation (1:15–20), the mystery of Christ in you as the hope of glory (1:27), and the fullness of deity in Christ as the demolition of every religious supplement (2:9–15). Chapters 3–4 are ethical: if Christ is everything, if you have died and been raised with him, if your life is hidden with him in God, then certain things must be put to death and certain things must be put on. The theology of chapters 1–2 always produces the ethics of chapters 3–4 in Pauline thought. Indicative before imperative; who you are before what you do.

The Christ hymn of Colossians 1:15–20 is one of the most majestic texts in the entire New Testament. In six verses it covers the entire scope of Christ’s lordship: he is the image of the invisible God; the firstborn over all creation; the one through whom, for whom, and in whom all things were created and cohere; the head of the body; the firstborn from the dead; the one in whom all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell; the one through whom God reconciled all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross. This is not merely elevated religious poetry; it is the most comprehensive christological statement in Paul’s letters, and it provides the theological foundation for everything else the letter argues. If Christ is who the hymn says he is, then the Colossian heresy — and every supplement to Christ in every generation — is not merely unnecessary but absurd.

Did Paul write Colossians? Some scholars doubt it, pointing to vocabulary and style unlike his undisputed letters, to the soaring hymn of 1:15–20, and to its close relation to Ephesians. But the letter names Paul three times (1:1, 23; 4:18), closes with his own signature, and is tied by its list of names to Philemon, which almost no one doubts is his. Differences of style are well explained by the subject, a new error to answer, and by the help of a co-writer, Timothy (1:1). The church received it as Paul’s from the beginning, and the more likely conclusion is that he wrote it.

Colossians is the answer to every form of Christianity that adds to Christ. It speaks directly to the believer who feels that faith in Christ alone is not quite enough — that additional spiritual experiences, additional practices, additional revelations are needed for full access to God. The letter says: you have been filled in him. You are complete. The fullness you are seeking is already yours, in the one in whom all fullness dwells. Seek more of him — not more beyond him.

1.title: The Supremacy of Christ: Hymn, Mystery, and Ministry
1.overview:
Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus. Paul had never visited; the church was planted by Epaphras, a local man converted probably during Paul’s years in Ephesus. Now, writing from prison, Paul hears that teachers are offering the Colossians something “more”: secret knowledge, angelic powers to be honoured, food laws and festivals, and harsh treatment of the body (2:8–23). Paul’s answer is not a better technique but a bigger Christ.

Chapter 1 thanks God for their faith, love and hope, and prays that they will know God’s will so as to live worthily, strengthened by his power, thankful that the Father has already qualified, rescued, transferred, redeemed and forgiven them. Then comes the great hymn (vv. 15–20): Christ is the image of the invisible God, the Creator and sustainer of everything, including every spiritual power; the head of the church and firstborn from the dead; the one in whom all God’s fullness dwells, who made peace by the blood of his cross. Finally Paul applies it: you who were God’s enemies are reconciled, if you continue in the faith, and the great mystery now revealed is “Christ in you, the hope of glory”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Colossae, a church Paul had not founded himself; it was planted by Epaphras. Paul thanks God for their faith in Christ and their love for all believers, both springing from the hope stored up for them in heaven, which they heard in the gospel now bearing fruit across the world. He prays that God will fill them with knowledge of his will, so that they live in a way that honours the Lord, growing in good works and in knowing God, strengthened to endure with patience and joy, and thankful to the Father, who has rescued them from the power of darkness and brought them into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom they have redemption and forgiveness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Knowledge of God’s Will: Wisdom vs. Esoteric Speculation

Paul’s prayer for “knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (v. 9) directly counters the false teachers’ offer of special knowledge. The knowledge Paul seeks for the Colossians is not mystical or esoteric; it is practical and ethical: “so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord.” Reformed theology has always insisted that true wisdom is not the accumulation of specialized spiritual information but the God-given capacity to live well in the world as God has made it, according to God’s own revealed will. The wisdom from above, as James says (3:17), is “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits.” It is visible in life, not in the possession of secret knowledge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered a form of spiritual wisdom that was speculative, esoteric, and attainable only through special initiation. Paul’s prayer shows what genuine spiritual wisdom looks like: it produces fruit, builds endurance, and generates thanksgiving. Now: The contemporary church is perennially attracted to special spiritual knowledge — prophetic insights, mystical experiences, hidden wisdom that the ordinary believer does not possess. Paul’s prayer is the corrective: true knowledge of God’s will is measured not by the height of its claims but by the quality of life it produces. Does it make you fruitful? Does it make you endure? Does it make you thankful? Those are the tests.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace to you and peace from God our Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle by God’s will, writes with Timothy to the holy and faithful believers in Colossae.

By the will of God. Paul’s authority does not rest on the Colossians’ approval. He had never met them (2:1), so he states where it comes from.

Timothy. Co-sender, not co-author. The ministry is never solitary.

Saints and faithful. Hagioi, holy ones: set apart by God’s act, not by spiritual achievement. Faithful: persevering. Both are true; neither cancels the other.

Grace and peace. Grace the source, peace the fruit. The order cannot be reversed.

A textual note. Many manuscripts add “and the Lord Jesus Christ” to the greeting (KJV), as in Paul’s other letters. The earliest have the shorter form.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ, you are a “saint” today, not because you feel holy but because God set you apart.
verseByVerse.note: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had never visited; the church was founded by Epaphras. Paul wrote from prison, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon.

verseByVerse.quote: We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God for them whenever he prays.

Thanks for people. Not for weather or success, but for God’s work in human lives. Every sign of grace in another person is God’s doing, so the Christian never runs short of reasons to thank him.

The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Not a philosophical abstraction or one god among many in the crowded market of Colossae, but the God revealed in Jesus. And the basis of our approach: the Father of the Lord Jesus is, by adoption, Father of all in him (John 20:17; Ephesians 1:3).

A pattern. The Father plans, the Son accomplishes, the Spirit applies, and the Father receives the thanks.

On a Tuesday. Before you pray for someone’s problems, thank God for something he has done in them.

verseByVerse.quote: since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has heard of their faith in Christ and their love for all the saints.

The two marks. Faith in Christ: the soul resting its whole weight on him. Love for all the saints: the evidence that the faith is real. Paul always looks for both (Galatians 5:6; 1 Thessalonians 1:3).

All the saints. Not just the congenial ones.

Inseparable. Faith that produces no love is not yet the real thing; love without faith in Christ has no inexhaustible source (1 John 4:20).

On a Tuesday. Which believer do you find hardest to love? That is where your faith is being tested this week.

verseByVerse.quote: because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their faith and love spring from the hope laid up for them in heaven, which they heard in the gospel.

Hope. Not a wish (“I hope it won’t rain”), but confident expectation: not uncertain, only unfinished. Specifically, the resurrection and full inheritance at Christ’s return (Romans 8:23–25; 3:4).

Laid up. A secured deposit, kept where nothing can spoil or steal it (1 Peter 1:4). Your circumstances may be terrible; your hope is untouched.

Hope fuels faith and love. Not the order of salvation, but what sustains them day by day. A believer who loses sight of what is coming finds faith shrinking and love cooling. The martyr, the missionary in the hard place, the Christian who keeps forgiving are all drawing on hope.

The word of truth. Against teaching that paraded as higher wisdom, Paul does not offer a rival philosophy. The gospel is true: it corresponds to what God has actually done.

Gospel. Euangelion, the word for imperial announcements of a victory or an heir: public, authoritative news demanding a response (Isaiah 52:7).

For worship. What is stored for you in heaven cannot be confiscated, burgled or devalued.

verseByVerse.quote: which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel is bearing fruit and growing throughout the world, as it has among them.

Alive. “Bearing fruit and increasing”: the gospel is God’s living word, carrying within itself the power to produce what it announces. The seed has life in itself; the farmer sows (Mark 4:26–29). “My word … shall not return to me empty” (Isaiah 55:11; Acts 12:24). We carry it; it works (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

The whole world. Its spread across the known world of Paul’s day, and its nature as a message for all nations; not that every people had heard (compare v. 23).

Understood. Epegnōte: not merely heard information but a full, life-reordering recognition.

The grace of God. To understand grace is to understand that you brought nothing, deserved nothing, and received everything.

In truth. Aimed at the false teachers, who said the Colossians needed something deeper. Paul says they already have the real thing. Nothing is lacking in a plain reception of the gospel (Galatians 1:6–9).

On a Tuesday. You do not have to make the gospel work. Share it, and trust it to do what it does.

verseByVerse.quote: just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf
verseByVerse.commentary:
They learned it from Epaphras, Christ’s faithful minister.

Epaphras. A Colossian (4:12), probably converted in Ephesus during Paul’s long stay, when “all the residents of Asia heard the word” (Acts 19:10). He took the gospel home to the Lycus Valley.

Fellow servant. Syndoulos, co-slave: the same Master, the same total obligation. Not a degradation but the highest honour.

Minister. Diakonos, a table-servant. In a status-obsessed world, the Christian leader waits at tables (Mark 10:44–45).

Of Christ. When Paul speaks of the source of salvation he names the Father (v. 3); when he speaks of the ministry’s commission and content, he names Christ, who sends (Matthew 28:18–20).

A textual note. Manuscripts divide between “on your behalf” (KJV, NIV) and “on our behalf” (ESV, following the earliest). If “our”, Epaphras served the Colossians as Paul’s representative, confirming that what they learned from him is Paul’s gospel.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the person who first taught you the gospel. Then ask who you might teach.
verseByVerse.note: Epaphras was a native of Colossae who probably heard the gospel during Paul’s long stay in Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: and has made known to us your love in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras has told Paul of their love in the Spirit.

Love in the Spirit. Not love that feels spiritual, but love whose source and energy is the Holy Spirit: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5). Love is the first fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22).

Two kinds of love. Natural love, for friends and family and people like us, is real and good, but it falters under pressure and dries up when not returned. Love in the Spirit draws on God’s supply, so it can love the difficult, the undeserving, the enemy.

The evidence. Anyone can adopt new beliefs. Not everyone starts loving people they would not naturally love. When Epaphras reported their love, Paul heard: the Spirit is at work (1 John 4:7).

On a Tuesday. Ask the Spirit for love for one specific difficult person, and then act as if he has given it.

verseByVerse.quote: And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that God will fill them with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and understanding.

Paul prays, not only explains. You can explain truth accurately and the hearer still not receive it. Understanding that changes a life is God’s gift (1 Corinthians 2:14). The best teachers pray hardest; Epaphras is “always struggling on your behalf in his prayers” (4:12).

Three terms. Knowledge of his will (epignōsis): a deep, practical grasp of what God wants. Spiritual wisdom: given by the Spirit, not human cleverness, which is exactly what the false teachers were selling, and found in Christ (2:3). Understanding (sunesis): seeing how things fit and applying them.

Which job, which spouse? Paul means God’s revealed will: how to live worthily (v. 10). Within it, God gives freedom to choose wisely, praying, seeking counsel and weighing what is good. He guides by his word and providence, not usually by special messages.

Against secret knowledge. The test of true spiritual knowledge is not the height of its claims but the life it produces (James 3:17).

On a Tuesday. Facing a decision? Ask what Scripture commands, seek wise counsel, pray, and then choose freely.

verseByVerse.quote: so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowledge is for living a life worthy of the Lord, fruitful and growing.

So as to walk. The grammar is explicit: knowledge and wisdom so that they live worthily. Prayer is the engine of discipleship, not a supplement.

Pleasing him. Because he loves us, not so that he will (1 John 4:19).

Every good work. The whole texture of daily life: the honest word when a lie would be easier, patience when irritation is natural, kindness to the person nobody notices.

Growing in the knowledge of God. A relationship deepening, not information piling up. And a spiral: knowing God produces worthy living, and worthy living deepens knowledge. “If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know” (John 7:17). The one who forgives learns something of grace he did not know before.

No ceiling. The elder of forty years still has more of God to know. To stop growing is not to stand still but to drift (2 Peter 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: being strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that God’s glorious power will strengthen them for endurance and patience with joy.

Being strengthened. Passive and continuous: an ongoing supply from outside, not a deposit at conversion to live off. Paul does not pray that they try harder.

The measure. “All power, according to his glorious might”: the power that raised Christ (Ephesians 1:19–20). Whoever thinks he needs only a little help has not counted what real love and forgiveness cost.

What for? Not spectacular gifts, but the quiet ones. Hypomonē, endurance under circumstances: the runner who keeps going. Makrothymia, patience with people: not retaliating, waiting for God to act.

With joy. Not forced cheerfulness, but the gladness of knowing God is sovereign and the inheritance secure (James 1:2–4; Romans 5:3–5).

On a Tuesday. If you are exhausted by a long trial, ask not for escape first but for endurance, patience and joy. That is what Paul asked for.

verseByVerse.quote: giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They should give thanks to the Father, who has qualified them to share the saints’ inheritance in light.

Qualified. Hikanōsanti, made fit, made sufficient. Pointed: the false teachers suggested believers were not yet fully qualified without extra experiences, angelic mediators or ascetic practices (2:18, 23). God has already qualified you, fully, not provisionally. Nothing to add.

Inheritance. Israel’s word for the promised land (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 32:9), transformed in Christ into sharing God’s life, the new creation, his face seen (1 Corinthians 2:9). Inherited by relationship, not earned (Romans 8:17).

In light. God’s presence, for God is light (1 John 1:5; Revelation 21:23). Set against the darkness of v. 13: two kingdoms, two destinations.

A textual note. Manuscripts divide between “qualified you” and “qualified us”, and a few read “called” instead of “qualified”. The ESV’s reading is well supported.

For worship. You are not on probation. Thank the Father who made you fit.

verseByVerse.quote: He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has rescued us from the domain of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son.

Delivered. A rescue word, used of God snatching Israel from Egypt. Not for someone who found his own way out, but for one trapped and pulled free (Ephesians 2:1–5).

The domain of darkness. Exousia, a word of government: a realm with a ruler, “the ruler of this world” (John 12:31), “the god of this world” (2 Corinthians 4:4). It feels normal from inside. The person in it does not feel trapped, which is part of the darkness.

Transferred. A completed act. Ancient conquerors moved whole populations to new lands; God has moved you. You are already a citizen of another kingdom while your feet stand on the old earth (Philippians 3:20). The kingdom has a glorious visible completion still to come, but the transfer has happened.

His beloved Son. Literally “the Son of his love”, echoing “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17). You have been brought inside the Father’s love for the Son, and nothing can remove that love (John 17:23).

On a Tuesday. Living as a citizen of another kingdom: what does your King want from you today, at work or at home?

verseByVerse.quote: in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the Son we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

Redemption. Apolytrōsis, from the ransom of captives and slaves: bought free by someone else’s payment. We were held by sin, by debt to a holy God, by the domain of darkness, and could not pay. Christ paid, with his blood (Ephesians 1:7; 1 Peter 1:18–19). Not cheap grace, but the costliest.

Forgiveness. Aphesis, release: a claim dropped, a debt cancelled. Not pretending the offences did not happen, but declaring the charge answered and the record cleared (2:13–14).

One event, two angles. Redemption answers “How did we get free?” A price was paid. Forgiveness answers where we stand now: the record is clear (Romans 3:24–25).

In him. Present tense: “we have”. Not hoped for; possessed, in Christ.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts add “through his blood” (KJV), from Ephesians 1:7. The earliest lack it. The doctrine is not affected; Paul says it in v. 20.

For worship. Your debt is not reduced or deferred. It is gone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In what may be an early Christian hymn, Paul describes who Christ is. He makes the invisible God visible. He holds the rank of the firstborn over all creation, because everything, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, including every spiritual power, was made through him and for him. He existed before all things and holds them together. He is also head of the church, the first to rise from the dead, so that he has first place in everything. The whole fullness of God was pleased to live in him, and through him God made peace with all things by the blood of his cross.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ as Creator and Redeemer: The Cosmic Scope of the Gospel

The Reformed tradition has always insisted on the unity of Christ’s work as both the agent of creation and the author of redemption. The hymn of Colossians 1:15–20 grounds this insistence: the same one through whom all things were made is the one through whose blood all things are reconciled. This means that redemption is not the rescue of souls from a material world that God has abandoned; it is the renewal of the entire creation that God originally made through Christ. The scope of the atonement is cosmic, not merely individual; the goal of redemption is “all things,” not merely individual souls. Abraham Kuyper’s famous claim — “there is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is Sovereign over all, does not cry: ‘Mine!’” — is exegetically grounded here.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian heresy apparently involved a hierarchy of spiritual powers — angels, thrones, dominions, rulers — through whom one had to navigate to reach God. The hymn annihilates this hierarchy: all these powers were created by Christ, are sustained by Christ, and are subject to Christ. There is no mediating hierarchy between the believer and God; Christ is the direct and only mediator. Now: Every form of Christianity that introduces additional mediators — saints, angels, spiritual powers, ecclesiastical hierarchies — between the believer and God is doing what the Colossian heresy did. The hymn says: Christ is the image of the invisible God. To see God, look at Christ. To reach God, come through Christ. There is no other way, no additional hierarchy, no further mediation required.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ is the visible image of the invisible God and ranks first over all creation.

A bigger Christ. For fourteen verses Paul prayed; now he speaks only of Christ until v. 20. His answer to false teaching is not a deeper secret but a bigger Christ. Keep him in focus and rivals shrink to their true size.

A hymn. Verses 15–20 have the balance of a hymn, perhaps sung in the churches. Two halves: Christ and creation (15–17), Christ and the new creation (18–20), linked by “firstborn”.

Image. Eikōn: not a faint likeness, but the exact, living self-expression of the original. No one has seen God (John 1:18), yet “whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9; Hebrews 1:3). Three echoes: the emperor’s image on a coin (Mark 12:16); humanity made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27), which Christ is truly, as the last Adam; and Jewish wisdom writing, which called Wisdom an image of God’s goodness.

Firstborn of all creation. Jehovah’s Witnesses and the ancient Arians read this as “the first being created”. Three answers. “Firstborn” means the pre-eminent heir: David, Jesse’s youngest son, is God’s “firstborn” (Psalm 89:27); Israel is God’s “firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22). Rank, not birth order. “Of” means over all creation, not part of it. And v. 16 says all things were created through him; a created being cannot create all created things.

For worship. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: “Firstborn” speaks of rank and supremacy, as the heir held first place — not that the Son was created.

parallels.desc: I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth

verseByVerse.quote: For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities — all things were created through him and for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things, visible and invisible, including every power, were created by him and for him.

The whole Trinity creates. From the Father (1 Corinthians 8:6), through the Son (John 1:3), by the Spirit (Genesis 1:2). Christ is spotlighted because he was being demoted to one power among many (2:18). Paul plants him on the Creator’s side of the line.

Visible and invisible. The decisive stroke, because the unseen realm was where the error located its powers.

Thrones, dominions, rulers, authorities. The vocabulary of angelic ranks the false teachers arranged into a hierarchy controlling access to God. Paul is not teaching a doctrine of angelic grades; he borrows their impressive list and sweeps it all into one sentence: created by Christ.

The pastoral point. You do not tremble before what your Lord made. Even the fallen powers, disarmed at the cross (2:15; Ephesians 6:12), are creatures, and their Maker is their Master. There is no dark kingdom fighting him on equal terms.

For him. Elsewhere all things are for the Father (Romans 11:36); here, for Christ: a quiet claim to full deity. You were not made to be your own end.

On a Tuesday. A key is made for one lock: forced into the wrong door, it jams; in the right one, it turns. The van you drive, the shelves you stack, the patience with a difficult colleague, done consciously for Christ, is what you were made for (3:23).
verseByVerse.note: Thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities are unseen spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ existed before all things, and holds all things together.

Before. In time: he existed before anything was made. And the tense is present, “he is before”, like “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). And in rank: above all things. The false teachers fitted Christ into the created order, one exalted being among the powers. Christ is not on the ladder; he made it.

Hold together. Synestēken: to cohere, to keep from flying apart, “has held and goes on holding”. Created through him (agency); held together in him (ongoing centre). Not a watchmaker who wound the world and walked away: “he upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3).

Withdraw his hand. Reality would not stop; it would unravel into nothing (Acts 17:28).

What it does not mean. Not that natural causes are unreal. Gravity and chemistry are the regular ways Christ holds things together. Science describes his faithfulness.

For worship. The Christ who keeps galaxies from flying apart holds your life together too, on the day it feels as though everything is coming apart.

verseByVerse.quote: And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ is head of the church, the first to rise from the dead, so that he is pre-eminent in everything.

Head. Kephalē carried both source (a river’s head) and authority (ruler). Christ is the source of the church’s life and its ruler. Greeks compared a community to a body; Paul says the church is Christ’s body, with Christ its living Head.

Why here? To bring the hymn home: the cosmic Lord of vv. 15–17 is Head of this small congregation. And against the error: the church has one Head; going elsewhere is “not holding fast to the Head” (2:19).

The beginning. Archē: first and source of the new creation that dawned at the empty tomb.

Firstborn from the dead. Others were raised before (Luke 7:14–15; John 11:43–44), but to mortal life, to die again. Christ was the first to pass through death into deathless life, the eldest brother of a great family who will follow (1 Corinthians 15:20; Romans 8:29). The empty tomb is a promissory note with your name on it.

Preeminent. Prōteuōn, holding first place, in everything. The Colossian error was a quiet demotion: Christ high, but sharing the platform. God’s purpose is that his Son be first (Philippians 2:9–11).

On a Tuesday. A wedding ring does not mean you love nothing else, but that one person comes first and everything else is arranged around her. A life is put right not by adding Christ to your list, but by moving him to the head of it.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the fullness of God was pleased to dwell in Christ.

The fullness. The Greek says simply “all the fullness”; the ESV rightly supplies “of God”, since 2:9 says “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily”.

Dwell. Katoikēsai: to settle, take up permanent residence, not lodge as a visitor. God did not merely visit Christ or work through a favoured man or rest on him like a prophet. The whole of God took up residence in him, bodily (John 1:14). God dwelt in the tabernacle symbolically, and dwells in believers by the Spirit; this is of another order.

Their own slogan. Plērōma was almost certainly a prized word of the false teachers, who pictured God’s fullness spread across a chain of intermediary beings, to be climbed rung by rung. Paul turns it: all the fullness is in Christ. The ladder is not just unnecessary; it insults the Son.

Was pleased. Eudokēsen, glad good pleasure: the root of “with whom I am well pleased”.

On a Tuesday. Imagine working for years at a vast firm, never meeting the owner, getting his mind second-hand down a chain, and then one Monday he pulls up a stool and says, “I’ve come myself.” That is what God did in Christ. To have Christ is to have all of God there is to have.

verseByVerse.quote: and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Christ’s blood on the cross God reconciles all things to himself, making peace.

Reconcile. Apokatallaxai, intensified: to bring enemies all the way home. The breach was on our side, yet the offended party moves first (2 Corinthians 5:18–19; Romans 5:10).

Through him. The same phrase as creation (v. 16). The hands that flung the stars were nailed to the beam. The Maker did not send the means; he became it.

All things. As wide as creation. When Adam fell, creation was “subjected to futility” and groans (Romans 8:20–22). The rescue is as large as the wreck.

Does everyone get saved? No. Universalists read “all things” as every person. Paul guards it three verses on: “if indeed you continue in the faith” (v. 23). Reconciliation here is the restoring of order to the cosmos, in two ways: glad children welcomed home, and hostile powers pacified, disarmed, put under his feet (2:15). Every knee will bow, some in joy, some in defeat (Philippians 2:10–11).

Made peace. Not a ceasefire but wholeness. There was real war: God’s wrath against sin, our hostility. God satisfied his justice and absorbed his wrath in his Son, so the peace is righteous, not cheap (Romans 5:1).

The blood of his cross. Blood: a life given in sacrificial death (Leviticus 17:11). The cosmic vision lands on a splinter of wood outside a city wall. The cosmic Lord is the crucified Saviour, and his throne is shaped like a cross.

A textual note. Some manuscripts omit the second “through him” before “whether on earth”. Its presence is better attested and adds emphasis.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — Reconciled and the Mystery Revealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Colossians were once estranged from God and hostile, as their actions showed. Now God has reconciled them through Christ’s physical death, in order to present them holy and blameless before him, provided they keep firmly to the gospel they heard. Paul rejoices in suffering for their sake, sharing in the hardships that come to Christ’s people, as the servant entrusted with making God’s word fully known. That word is a mystery hidden for ages and now revealed: Christ among the Gentiles, and in them, the hope of glory. Paul proclaims Christ, warning and teaching everyone, to present everyone mature in him, and he labours at it with the energy Christ supplies.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery of Christ in You: Union with Christ as the Heart of the Gospel

The phrase “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (v. 27) is the most compressed statement of the doctrine of union with Christ in the New Testament. The mystery that was hidden for ages is not merely that Gentiles would be included in the covenant people (though that is part of it); it is that Christ himself would take up residence in his people — that the indwelling of the Spirit would mean the indwelling of Christ himself in the hearts of those who believe. Reformed theology has always understood union with Christ as the foundation of all soteriological benefits: it is because believers are in Christ that they are justified, sanctified, and will be glorified. And it is because Christ is in believers that they have the living presence of the hope of glory dwelling within them now.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that they needed additional spiritual experiences and esoteric knowledge to be “complete” or “mature.” Paul says: the mystery that makes for maturity is already in you. Christ in you is the hope of glory. The treasure the false teachers are selling is already yours, in a far more intimate and certain form than they can offer. Now: The believer who feels spiritually incomplete, who is seeking a second blessing, a higher experience, a deeper initiation, needs to hear this: Christ is in you. The one in whom all fullness dwells is dwelling in you by his Spirit. The seeking is not wrong; but what you are seeking is already present. Seek to know more fully the one who is already yours.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once they were alienated from God and hostile in mind.

And you. The camera turns from the cosmos to the reader. “All things” includes you.

“I was never a bad person.” Paul is not saying every unbeliever is a monster. Many outside Christ are warm and honest. He measures people not against each other but against God: is the life turned towards its Maker or away? Every life outside Christ, however decent, is lived with its back to God.

Alienated. Estranged from the fellowship we were made for, “without God in the world” (Ephesians 2:12; 4:18). “Once”: for the believer, a country left for good.

Hostile in mind. Not that every unbeliever consciously hates God; most never think of him. The natural mind will not have him on the throne: “the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God” (Romans 8:7). Polite indifference and open scorn are two faces of one enmity.

Evil deeds. The symptom, not the disease. We do wrong because we are alienated. Even kind acts done without reference to God are offered by a heart turned away (Isaiah 64:6).

On a Tuesday. Think of the most decent man on your old street, who paid his bills, lent his ladder and said, “I’m not religious; I just do no harm.” That sentence is v. 21: not raging against heaven, simply running his own little kingdom with God nowhere in it. That was every one of us. Which makes the next word blaze: “now”.

verseByVerse.quote: he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ has reconciled them by his death, to present them holy and blameless before God.

Once, now. One word marks the great divide of a life.

He. God is the subject. We brought nothing but the hostility needing reconciliation. Not God meeting us halfway, but crossing the whole distance (2 Corinthians 5:18–19).

Finished. “He has reconciled”: done, at the cross, where Jesus said “It is finished” (John 19:30). You do not wake each morning to re-earn God’s welcome; you live from a settled peace.

In his body of flesh. Against spiritualisers who would find salvation through a bleeding body embarrassing. And the Christ in whom deity dwells bodily (2:9) had to become flesh to die for flesh (Hebrews 10:10). Our peace cost God a body.

Present. Paristēmi: to bring forward, as a bride to the altar or an offering before God. Holy: wholly God’s. Blameless: amōmos, the word for an unblemished lamb. Above reproach: a courtroom word, no charge will stick.

“I don’t feel holy.” This is your standing, not your feeling: Christ’s record credited to you, your sin counted his (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 8:33–34). And what you are now by reckoning, you will be in full (Jude 24; Philippians 1:6). Your sense of falling short is the gap between standing and experience, and its closing rests on God’s grip on you.

A textual note. Some early manuscripts read “you were reconciled” (passive), others “he has reconciled”. Either way, God does it.

verseByVerse.quote: if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must continue in the faith, not shifting from the hope of the gospel.

A real “if”. Those presented holy are those who keep believing. A faith that finally collapses and walks away was never the living thing it seemed (1 John 2:19).

But God keeps. The continuing is God’s gift: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6); “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28); “by God’s power” they are “being guarded through faith” (1 Peter 1:5). The saints persevere because God preserves them.

Can a true believer be lost? Arminian Christians read the “if” as a condition a believer may fail, pointing to Hebrews 6:4–6. The warning is real. But Paul has just said God reconciled them in order to present them blameless. The more likely reading is that continuing is the evidence of true faith and the means God uses to bring his people home.

The climber. Roped to an expert guide, he must keep climbing, and his effort is real. When his boot slips, the rope holds. The “if” is not meant to torment you with “do I have enough faith?”, but to summon you to keep going.

Stable, steadfast, not shifting. Building words: founded, bolted down, not budged. The false teachers were trying to move them onto “deeper” teaching.

In all creation. Not a census claim, but the gospel’s public, worldwide character, against a secret for an inner circle.

Minister. Servant, not master. He serves the gospel; he did not invent it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul rejoices in his sufferings, sharing in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of the church.

From prison. “Remember my chains” (4:18). His life was a catalogue of hardship (2 Corinthians 11:23–28).

Why rejoice? Not masochism. The suffering is for people he loves; it draws him into fellowship with Christ (Philippians 3:10; Acts 5:41); and through a prison cell the gospel runs free.

What it cannot mean. That Christ’s atoning suffering was insufficient. Paul has just said peace was made “by the blood of his cross” (v. 20). To Christ’s sin-bearing not one drop can be added.

What it does mean. Two kinds of suffering are bound up with Christ: his once-for-all atoning death, which we receive but never share; and his afflictions in his suffering people as the gospel advances. Christ is so joined to his church that to strike it is to strike him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). A measure of such affliction remains before the end, and Paul takes his share.

A Roman Catholic reading. This verse has been used to support a treasury of merit to which the saints’ sufferings add, and offering up sufferings for others’ benefit. But Paul never says Christ’s atonement was incomplete. His sufferings serve the church’s growth, not the price of anyone’s forgiveness.

On a Tuesday. When you bear loss or scorn for Christ, it is not wasted misfortune. Paul’s cell was not a dead end; it was a pulpit (Philippians 1:12–14).
verseByVerse.note: Paul does not mean Christ’s atoning suffering was incomplete; he shares in the afflictions that Christ’s people must still endure.

verseByVerse.quote: of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made Paul a servant of the church to make known his word in full, the mystery hidden for ages.

Stewardship. Oikonomia: the trusted manager of a great household, holding the keys to dispense the master’s provisions. He does not own them, did not appoint himself, and must give account (1 Corinthians 4:1–2). “Given to me for you”: for their benefit, not his prestige.

From God. All through this passage everything descends: the gospel, the mystery, its revealing, the stewardship, the strength (v. 29). Nothing ascends from earth.

Fully known. The whole counsel of God, nothing edited (Acts 20:27), carried to its full reach among the Gentiles. The false teachers wanted to add; Paul says it is already full.

The word of God. Here the gospel message (v. 5), God’s own authoritative word (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

Mystery. Not a puzzle, but a secret once hidden in God’s mind and now openly told (v. 27). Paul takes the false teachers’ favourite word and turns it inside out: God’s secret is published to all.

Hidden, yet there. In shadow in the Old Testament: the serpent-crusher (Genesis 3:15), blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:3), a light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6). Like a letter addressed to you, lying sealed for generations until opened (Romans 16:25–26).

To his saints. All believers, not an inner circle (Matthew 11:25).
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mystery is Christ in you, the hope of glory, even among the Gentiles.

God chose. He could have kept his secret and wronged no one. He chose to tell, and to tell outsiders and rebels (Matthew 11:26).

Among the Gentiles. To Jewish minds they were “strangers to the covenants of promise … without God in the world” (Ephesians 2:12). That they would become the showroom of God’s glory no one saw coming (Ephesians 3:6). The Colossians are those Gentiles: this is about you. The death of spiritual snobbery.

The riches of the glory. Words piling up because the thing is too large.

A Person. The treasure is “Christ in you”: not Christ far above, reached by a ladder of angels, but the living Lord by his Spirit in the humblest believer (Galatians 2:20; Romans 8:9–10). “In you” is plural, “among you” as a church, and each believer.

The hope of glory. Because Christ is in you now, glory is certain: “when Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (3:4).

On a Tuesday. Imagine a king leaving his palace to move into a labourer’s cottage, not to visit but to live. The neighbours ask, why there? But if the King has moved into your cottage now, he certainly means to bring you home to his palace. “Christ in you” is the King in the cottage; “the hope of glory” is the palace that must follow.

verseByVerse.quote: Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul proclaims Christ, warning and teaching everyone, to present everyone mature in Christ.

Him. First and emphatic in the Greek. Not a code, a system or a ladder of disciplines, but a Person. Against regulations, festivals, food laws and angel-rituals, Paul heralds a Master. You do not get Christ by keeping the rules; you get the rules kept by having Christ (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Proclaim. Katangellomen, a herald’s public announcement, not a whispered initiation.

Warning. Nouthetountes: counselling someone out of harm’s way, as Paul did at Ephesus “with tears” (Acts 20:31). A shepherd who never mentions the cliff is not kind but faithless.

Teaching with all wisdom. The wisdom found in Christ (2:3), fitted to each real life.

Everyone, three times. Against a heresy that hoarded secrets for an inner ring.

Mature. Teleios, full-grown. Not sinless, not mere head-knowledge, not an elite tier. Rooted, steady, discerning, Christlike, able to feed yourself from God’s word (Ephesians 4:13–15; Hebrews 5:13–14). A sapling and an oak share the same life; the oak is that life grown full.

On a Tuesday. Are you growing up, or still on milk after years? Find someone to read Scripture with you.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this Paul toils with all the energy Christ powerfully works in him.

I toil. From “we proclaim” to “I toil”: what the goal costs him, in a cell (4:18), for churches he has never met.

For this. To present everyone mature in Christ. Not fame, not converts left as babies.

Hard work. Kopiō, to labour bone-weary; agōnizomenos, an athlete straining, behind “agonise”. The Christian life is not an effortless drift.

His energy. Paul strains every muscle, but with God’s power working inside him: “work out your own salvation … for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13). Not fifty-fifty: fully Paul’s striving and fully God’s working (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Two ditches. “Let go and let God”, which treats all effort as unspiritual, breeds passivity and fruitless faith. “It’s all up to me”, white-knuckled willpower, breeds pride or burnout: self-reliance in religious clothes.

On a Tuesday. A sailing crew must hoist the sails and trim the lines, but it is the wind that drives the boat, and the wind fills only sails that have been set. So set the sails: pray, fight sin, feed on the Word, serve. Work hard, and lean hard.
