2.title: Fullness in Christ: Warnings Against Every Supplement
2.overview:
Now Paul names the danger. Teachers are offering the Colossians a “philosophy” that sounds wise: keep food laws and holy days, practise harsh self-denial, honour angels as mediators, and pursue visions. Its message is “Christ plus”. Paul answers in three steps. First, stay rooted in Christ, as you received him, because all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him. Second, in him the whole fullness of God dwells bodily, and you are filled in him. You have already been circumcised, buried and raised with him; God made you alive, forgave all your sins, cancelled the record of debt by nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the spiritual powers, leading them in triumph.

Third, therefore let no one judge you over food or holy days, which were shadows of Christ, the substance. Let no one disqualify you with self-made severity, angel worship and visions: such people have let go of the Head, from whom the whole body grows. Rules like “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch” look wise but have no power to stop the flesh. The cure for sin is not more rules but union with the risen Christ, which chapter 3 unfolds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Rooted and Built Up in Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul wants them to know how hard he is striving for them, for Laodicea and for others who have never met him, so that they may be encouraged, united in love, and rich in understanding of God’s mystery, which is Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. He says this so that no one deceives them with persuasive talk. Though absent, he rejoices at their good order and firm faith. As they received Christ Jesus as Lord, so they should go on living in him, rooted, built up, established in the faith and overflowing with thanks.
verseByVerse.theology:
All the Treasures of Wisdom Hidden in Christ

Colossians 2:3 — “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” — is the epistemological foundation of the Reformed tradition’s approach to all knowledge. Cornelius Van Til’s presuppositionalism, Abraham Kuyper’s sphere sovereignty, Francis Schaeffer’s integrated Christian worldview: all are ultimately grounded in this text. All genuine wisdom and knowledge find their coherence and source in Christ. This does not mean that only Christians can know things; it means that all knowledge that is genuinely true is “thinking God’s thoughts after him,” participating (knowingly or not) in the structure of reality that Christ created and sustains. The Christian intellectual task is to follow wisdom wherever it leads, knowing that it leads ultimately to the one in whom all wisdom is hidden.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy offered esoteric wisdom that seemed to go beyond what the gospel provided. Paul says: all the wisdom you are seeking is already hidden in Christ. You are not lacking wisdom; you have not been exploring deeply enough the one in whom wisdom dwells. Now: The Christian who turns to secular philosophy, psychology, or spirituality for the wisdom that Christ supposedly cannot provide has accepted the false teachers’ premise. All genuine wisdom, wherever it is found, is a trace of the one in whom all wisdom is hidden. The Christian engages with every source of wisdom while recognizing that Christ is its ultimate source and criterion.

verseByVerse.quote: For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is struggling in prayer for churches he has never visited.

Strangers he loves. Paul had never been to Colossae; Epaphras planted it (1:7). He agonises for people he would not recognise in the street. A hireling cares for what the flock does for him; a shepherd cares for the flock (John 10:12–13).

Laodicea. Ten miles away, sharing the same danger (4:16). Later, the lukewarm church of Revelation 3:14–22.

Struggle. Agōn, the wrestler’s all-out effort, as in 1:29. In chains (4:18), he cannot visit. He struggles chiefly on his knees, like Epaphras, “always struggling on your behalf in his prayers” (4:12).

On a Tuesday. Somewhere an unseen believer may be praying for you by name. And this is what love looks like: labouring before God for a soul you may never meet. Choose a missionary or persecuted church and pray for them this week.
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea lay about 10 miles from Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He wants them encouraged, united in love, and rich in full understanding of God’s mystery, Christ.

What he asks. Not comfort or growth in numbers, but three deeper things.

Hearts encouraged. Paraklēthōsin: braced, given courage to stand against persuasive arguments (v. 4). The “heart” is the whole inner person.

Knit together in love. Woven into one body. The lone sheep is picked off; the knit flock stands. Heresy isolates and flatters the few; love weaves the whole body together, and understanding grows in that soil.

Full assurance. Plērophoria: settled certainty, resting on actually understanding the truth, not a leap in the dark.

The mystery is Christ. Not a secret doctrine but a Person (1:26–27). The false teachers dangled “knowledge”, “mystery” and “fullness” as prizes beyond Christ. Paul says they are Christ.

A textual note. This phrase has more manuscript variations than almost any in Paul: “of God, Christ”; “of God the Father of Christ”; “of God and the Father and of Christ” (KJV), and others. Scribes evidently tried to clarify an abrupt phrase. The short “of God, Christ” best explains the others and is likely original.

For worship. God’s desire is not that you be clever or initiated, but sure.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ.

Treasures. What people dig, dive and travel the world to find. Knowledge (understanding God and reality) and wisdom (the skill of living in its light): all of it stored in Christ.

Hidden. Apokryphoi: not locked away from God’s people, but treasured up, as gold in a vault. Christ is God’s strongroom.

Their word, turned. The false teachers peddled “hidden” wisdom for the initiated, reached by climbing past Christ. All the truly hidden treasures are in Christ, who is “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). You do not graduate from Christ; you go deeper into him.

Can unbelievers know truth? Yes. By common grace they discover much that is true, and Christians may learn from them. Paul means the wisdom that saves and makes sense of everything, found only in Christ. All truth is God’s truth, and coheres in him.

On a Tuesday. A man spends years chasing treasure schemes, then a lawyer tells him the deed to the richest mine in the country was made out in his name long ago. That is you and Christ (Matthew 13:44). You are not a second-class believer outside the vault.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul says this so that no one deceives them with persuasive arguments.

Why the Christ-hymn. Paul reveals why he pressed Christ’s sufficiency so hard: a danger is circling.

The Colossian error. A blend of Jewish rule-keeping (food laws, holy days, perhaps circumcision, 2:11, 16), harsh self-denial, angel worship and claims to visions (2:18). Its method was not to deny Christ but to add to him.

Delude. Paralogizētai: to deceive by false reasoning, as a swindler reasons a man out of his money.

Plausible arguments. Pithanologia: persuasive speech. The peril is that error does not look false; it comes dressed as wisdom (v. 23).

The tell. The little word “plus”. Today: “Jesus, of course, but you also need this experience, this teacher’s system, these rules.” The guard: all the treasures are already in Christ (v. 3; 2 Corinthians 11:3).

On a Tuesday. When a teaching excites you, ask: does this make Christ bigger, or does it make him not quite enough?

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though absent, Paul rejoices in their good order and firm faith.

With you in spirit. Not mystical projection but love that leaps distance (1 Corinthians 5:3), and the deeper bond of one Spirit in all believers.

Rejoicing in chains. Over the health of a church he has never seen (3 John 4; 1 Thessalonians 3:8).

Battle words. “Good order”, taxis: troops drawn up in ranks. “Firmness”, stereōma: a battle line that holds. The church is under attack, yet the line holds.

Praise before warning. He commends a line that is holding before reinforcing it.

Faith in Christ. Their firmness rests on its object. The line holds because the one it leans on cannot be moved (1 Corinthians 15:58).

On a Tuesday. Before you correct someone, name what is strong in them.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they received Christ Jesus the Lord, they must walk in him, rooted, built up and overflowing with thanks.

Therefore. The hinge of the letter. Doctrine becomes duty.

Received Christ Jesus the Lord. Not a set of teachings but a Person, as Master. “Received” is the word for receiving a handed-down tradition (1 Corinthians 15:1–3).

So walk in him. The way you began is the way you go on. You came with empty hands, resting on Christ alone; keep walking that way. You do not move on from him; you go on in him: “Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3).

Rooted and built up. Mixed metaphors, garden and building site (Ephesians 3:17; 1 Corinthians 3:9). “Rooted” is perfect tense: planted once for all. “Built up” is present: being built daily. Anchored and rising.

As you were taught. By Epaphras (1:7). The mark of truth is faithfulness to what was handed down, not novelty (Jude 3).

Abounding in thanksgiving. A heart overflowing with thanks for what it already has in Christ has no appetite for “something more”. Ingratitude is the crack where discontent enters, and discontent is the heretic’s foothold.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts read “abounding in it with thanksgiving” (KJV). The shorter text is earlier.

On a Tuesday. Israel ate bread from heaven every morning and grumbled the whole way. Count your mercies aloud today. You cannot grumble and give thanks in the same breath.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to be captured by empty, deceptive philosophy rooted in human tradition and the world’s basic principles rather than in Christ. The whole fullness of God lives in Christ bodily, and believers are complete in him, who is head over every power. In him they have received a circumcision not done by hands, the stripping away of the old nature, and in baptism they were buried with him and raised with him through faith in God’s power. God made them alive with Christ, forgave all their sins, cancelled the record of debt that stood against them by nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the hostile powers, exposing them publicly and triumphing over them in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cancellation of the Debt and the Disarming of the Powers

Colossians 2:13–15 contains two of the most vivid metaphors for the atonement in the New Testament. First, the legal metaphor: the “record of debt” (cheirographon) that stood against us — the written bond of indebtedness, the document that recorded every sin and violation — has been cancelled, taken out of the way, nailed to the cross. The debt is not merely forgiven; the document is destroyed. Second, the military metaphor: the rulers and authorities who held humanity in their power through guilt and the law’s accusation have been “disarmed” and put to open shame — led in a triumphal procession like conquered enemies behind the victorious general. These two images together show what the cross accomplished: liberation from guilt (the debt cancelled) and liberation from spiritual bondage (the powers defeated).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy appealed to the elemental spirits and cosmic powers as real and threatening forces that needed to be placated through ritual observance. Paul says: those powers have been disarmed. They are defeated enemies, paraded in public shame behind the triumphing Christ. You do not placate them; you stand on the victory that has already been won. Now: The Christian who lives in fear of spiritual powers — who approaches life with anxiety about demonic influence, spiritual attack, or cosmic forces working against them — needs to hear this: the powers have been disarmed. Christ has triumphed. The fear of powers that have been publicly defeated is not piety; it is a failure to reckon with the victory of the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must not be taken captive by empty philosophy based on human tradition and the world’s elementary spirits rather than Christ.

See to it. A watchman’s cry: beware.

Takes you captive. Sylagōgōn: a slave-raider carrying off plunder. Seized physically, you would fight. Captured in the realm of ideas, the captive feels enlightened, not chained. Spiritual captivity wears the disguise of progress.

Philosophy. Not all careful thinking; Paul reasoned with philosophers at Athens (Acts 17:18–31). This particular system, hollow at the core.

Empty deceit. Promising fullness, delivering a void, while in Christ “you have been filled” (v. 10).

Human tradition. From men, not God: “you leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men” (Mark 7:8).

Elemental spirits. Stoicheia: either the basic principles of religion, or, more likely, the spiritual powers thought to rule through calendar and stars (Galatians 4:3, 9). Both readings are held.

Not according to Christ. The hinge. Christ is the measuring rod. You need not master every cult; you need to know one thing surpassingly well.

Should Christians avoid philosophy? No. Study it, and every field, testing all by Christ and his word.

On a Tuesday. Bank tellers learn to spot forgeries by handling genuine notes constantly. Know Christ deeply, and what diminishes him will feel wrong at once (1 John 4:1).
verseByVerse.note: “Elemental spirits” may mean the basic principles of religion or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily.

For. The reason for v. 8: nothing can be added to Christ, because all of God is in him.

The whole fullness. Pan to plērōma: nothing left over, nothing elsewhere.

Of deity. Theotētos, the strongest word available: not divine qualities, but Godhood itself. Christ is not a creature filled with attributes; the complete divine nature is in him.

Dwells. Katoikei, present: permanent residence, even now in his exalted state.

Bodily. Sōmatikōs: in a real human body (John 1:14). All of God, in a body you could have stood beside.

Three blows. Against angels and elemental spirits: they have no fullness to offer. Against fullness spread thin across a chain of beings: it is concentrated in Christ. Against contempt for the body: God dwells bodily in Christ.

For worship. In Christ you do not have a fragment of God or a junior deputy. You have all of God there is (1:19; John 14:9).

verseByVerse.quote: and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers have been filled in Christ, the head over every ruler and authority.

Fullness, filled. Plērōma in Christ (v. 9), peplērōmenoi in you: the same root. What is true of the Head overflows to the members.

Three things. Perfect tense: you have been filled and remain full. Passive: God did it. “In him”: by union, not attainment.

What it does not mean. Not sinless perfection, nor that you possess deity. You lack nothing for salvation, nothing for access to God, nothing for true completeness.

Head of all rule and authority. The powers the false teachers urged them to revere were created by Christ (1:16), will be disarmed by him (2:15), and are ruled by him. Not one outranks your Lord (Ephesians 1:21–22; Romans 8:38–39).

On a Tuesday. Like a man with a fortune in his account fretting that he is poor, you may feel like a second-rate Christian. The answer is not to earn more but to wake up to what is already yours.

verseByVerse.quote: In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ they were spiritually circumcised and, in baptism, buried and raised with him through faith.

The true circumcision. The false teachers pressed the physical rite. Paul says the real thing, always pointed to, was a circumcised heart: “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:6; Romans 2:28–29), done by God, “without hands”.

The body of the flesh. Not a scrap of skin, but the whole old sinful self cut away.

The circumcision of Christ. Either the circumcision Christ performs, or Christ’s own “cutting off” in death, which the believer shares. Both fit.

Buried and raised. Baptism portrays the old life put in Christ’s grave and a new life raised (Romans 6:3–4). The ground of 3:1.

Through faith. Not the water by itself, but God’s power received by faith. Faith is the empty hand; God raises.

Does baptism replace circumcision? Christians who baptise infants argue that circumcision was given to Abraham’s infant sons and Paul links it here with baptism, so the sign belongs to believers’ children. Serious arguments. But Paul says the circumcision meant is “without hands”, inward, and they were raised “through faith”. He does not say baptism replaces circumcision; he says Christ’s inward circumcision is what circumcision pointed to, and baptism signs it for those who believe. The more likely reading is believers’ baptism.

Does baptism save? Roman Catholic and Lutheran Christians hold God gives new birth through it. Paul ties rising to faith. Baptism is God’s sign and seal and a public confession, not effective apart from faith. Burial and rising fit immersion most naturally.

A textual note. Later manuscripts read “the body of the sins of the flesh” (KJV). The shorter text is earlier.

For worship. You cannot improve on death and resurrection. You have been through the grave and out the other side in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made them alive with Christ, forgiving all their sins and cancelling the record of debt at the cross.

Dead. Not sick or struggling: spiritual corpses (Ephesians 2:1). Dead in trespasses, and outside the covenant as Gentiles, with hearts not yet renewed.

Made alive together. Synezōopoiēsen: resurrection language. You do not improve a corpse; you raise it. Not God helping those who help themselves, but life given to those who had none (Ephesians 2:5).

All. Charisamenos, from “grace”. All: past, present and future, the ones that haunt you at three in the morning, the ones never confessed to a soul (Psalm 103:12; Micah 7:19). Not cheap: Christ bore every one.

The record of debt. Cheirographon: a handwritten IOU signed by the debtor. God’s ledger of every command broken, “with its legal demands”, beyond all paying.

Cancelled. Exaleiphō: to wash the ink off the page, as though never written (Isaiah 43:25).

Nailed to the cross. Romans nailed a criminal’s charge above his head; over Jesus, “King of the Jews” (John 19:19). Paul says our charge-sheet was nailed there. How? Because our debt was laid on Jesus (Isaiah 53:5–6; Galatians 3:13). He took it into the grave, and it never came back out. The empty tomb is the receipt.

Why confess, then? As Judge, God has forgiven us once for all (Romans 8:1). As Father, he wants us to confess sins that spoil fellowship (Matthew 6:12; 1 John 1:9). We confess not to stay saved, but because we are his children.

The law nailed? Some take the record to be the Mosaic law itself. More likely it is our signed guilt before the law. Either way, the law cannot condemn those in Christ; love still keeps God’s commandments (Romans 13:8–10).

A textual note. Manuscripts vary between “made you alive” and “made us alive”, and “forgave you” and “forgave us”. Paul includes himself either way.
verseByVerse.note: The “record of debt” was a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor; the charge against a crucified man was nailed above him.

verseByVerse.quote: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them.

The powers. Not human kings but spiritual forces, “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12): created by Christ (1:16), ruled by him (2:10), and feared and courted by the false teachers (2:18). They held humanity through sin, through accusation, and through fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15).

Disarmed. Stripped of weapons. Their great weapon was our guilt; the devil is “the accuser” (Revelation 12:10). Once the debt is cancelled (v. 14), the accuser has nothing to accuse with. The two verses are welded together.

The irony. The powers “crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8) and in that act were undone.

Triumphing. Thriambeusas, the Roman triumph: the victorious general in his chariot, enemy kings in chains behind him, paraded before jeering crowds. The cross, which looked like defeat, was the victory parade.

In him, or in it. The Greek can mean “in him” (Christ) or “in it” (the cross). Either way, the victory is at Calvary.

What it does not mean. Not that evil powers are imaginary or no longer active. They are real and beaten, like a fierce dog on a short chain, still barking and lunging, but unable to drag down one who belongs to the Victor (1 Peter 5:8; James 4:7).

On a Tuesday. You need not fear the dark or bargain with it. Stand in the finished victory (Romans 16:20).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman general celebrated victory by parading his captives through the streets.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So no one should judge them over food and drink, festivals, new moons or sabbaths; these were shadows of what was to come, and the reality is Christ. They must not let anyone disqualify them who insists on self-abasement, the worship of angels and claims of visions, puffed up by an unspiritual mind and not holding on to Christ the head, from whom the whole body grows. Since they died with Christ to the world’s basic principles, why submit to rules like “do not handle, do not taste”? Such regulations, based on human teaching, look wise with their strict religion and harsh treatment of the body, but they are powerless to restrain the flesh.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shadow and Substance: The Old Covenant as Anticipation

Paul’s description of the Mosaic observances as “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (v. 17) is the hermeneutical principle underlying all Reformed typological interpretation of the Old Testament. The ceremonial law — the festivals, the sabbaths, the food laws, the sacrificial system — was genuinely given by God and genuinely pointed forward to the reality that was coming. But it was always a shadow, not the substance; always anticipation, not fulfilment. The substance arrived in Christ. To return to the shadow when the substance is present is not faithfulness to the law; it is a failure to read what the law was always saying.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers were using Jewish observances as part of their syncretic system, insisting that the Colossians needed to keep certain days and food laws and festivals. Paul says: these were shadows pointing to Christ; Christ has come. Now: The same principle applies to any Christian movement that makes Old Testament ceremonial practices the standard of Christian spirituality. The principles of justice, love, and holiness that the ceremonial law expressed are fulfilled in Christ and applied by the Spirit. The specific ceremonies have been fulfilled in him who was their substance all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So no one may judge them over food, drink, festivals, new moons or Sabbaths.

Therefore. Because you are filled in Christ, the debt cancelled, the powers disarmed.

The rules. Clean and unclean food and drink, and the sacred calendar: “festival, new moon, Sabbath” is the Old Testament’s standard summary of yearly, monthly and weekly holy days (1 Chronicles 23:31; Hosea 2:11).

Pass judgment. Condemning them for not keeping these, making them feel second-class.

What it does not mean. Not that such observances are sinful; a believer may hold convictions about days and food (Romans 14:5–6). But they may not be made the measure of anyone’s standing with God.

The weekly Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession, hold Paul means only Israel’s ceremonial sabbaths, and that the weekly Sabbath remains a creation ordinance (Genesis 2:3), now kept on the Lord’s Day. But Paul’s triad names yearly, monthly and weekly days together. The more likely reading is that the weekly Sabbath is included, a shadow fulfilled in Christ, whose rest we enter (Hebrews 4:9–10). Christians gather on the first day as a glad and ancient practice (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10), a privilege rather than a law binding the conscience.

The modern version. “A real Christian never touches a drink”; this diet or fast to be holy; must (or must not) keep Christmas or Lent; only this translation, these songs, this schooling. Wherever something Christ left free becomes a test of acceptance, that is the Colossian heresy in a Sunday suit.

Both ways. Do not let anyone make you feel second-rate, and do not judge a brother who differs (Romans 14:1–4; Galatians 5:1).

verseByVerse.quote: These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These were shadows of what was to come; the substance belongs to Christ.

A shadow. The outline an object throws: its shape, none of its substance. The ceremonial law was a God-given shadow cast ahead of Christ (Hebrews 8:5; 10:1).

What each traced. The Passover lamb outlined the Lamb of God (1 Corinthians 5:7). The Day of Atonement, his once-for-all sacrifice. The Sabbath, the rest he gives (Matthew 11:28). The tabernacle, God dwelling with his people (John 1:14).

The substance. Literally “the body” (sōma): the solid body that threw the whole shadow is Christ. When your friend walks through the door, you do not keep staring at his silhouette on the wall.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is worthless. Shadows are real and God-given, and tell you something is coming. The moral law, which reflects God’s character, is not a shadow; the ceremonial law is.

For worship. Every feast and sacrifice was a finger tracing the shape of Jesus. Now the finger has found what it pointed at (Matthew 5:17; John 5:39).

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one may disqualify them by false humility, angel worship and claimed visions.

Disqualify. Katabrabeuō: an umpire ruling against a competitor and robbing him of the prize. The teachers set themselves up as judges of the Colossians’ faith.

Asceticism. Literally “delighting in humility”: self-imposed severity, harsh fasting, rough treatment of the body as a path to higher spirituality (v. 23). A performance of lowliness. Not an attack on genuine fasting, which Scripture commends, but on making bodily severity a badge of rank.

Worship of angels. Devotion to angels as mediators and guardians. It dethrones the one Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5). Angels refuse it: “You must not do that! … Worship God” (Revelation 19:10). Some read it as joining in the angels’ worship in visions; either way, it bypasses Christ.

Visions. Authority built on private experiences: “I have seen what you have not.” Spiritual one-upmanship.

A textual note. Later manuscripts read “intruding into those things which he hath not seen” (KJV), adding “not”. The earliest lack it: he goes on about what he has seen. The word embateuōn may be a term from initiation rites: “entering into” visions.

Puffed up by the flesh. The irony: the man who beats his body to escape the flesh is driven by the flesh’s craving for status. His “humility” is vanity in disguise.

On a Tuesday. Beware anyone who rates Christians by dramatic experiences, or slips angels or “spirit guides” between you and Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The false teaching seems to have mixed Jewish rules, strict self-denial and fascination with angels and visions.

verseByVerse.quote: and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such people are not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body grows with God-given growth.

Not holding fast. The diagnosis of the whole heresy: for all his visions and disciplines, the false teacher has let go of Christ, the Head (1:18).

From whom. The whole body draws life from the Head alone. Fed and knit together through joints and ligaments that both link the parts and carry the supply. The growth “is from God” (Ephesians 4:15–16; 1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

A picture. Cut a branch from the vine and it withers (John 15:5). The false teachers offered a fancier life while cutting the branch from its only source.

Two lessons. Growth is not a technique to master but the fruit of staying joined to Jesus, through faith, the Word and prayer. And you do not grow alone: Christ’s life runs through the connections to other believers. A Christian was never meant to be a severed limb.

On a Tuesday. Stop hunting for life in programmes. Hold on to Christ, and stay connected to his people.

verseByVerse.quote: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations— “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having died with Christ, they must not submit to human rules that have an appearance of wisdom but cannot restrain the flesh.

You died. Not a doubt but a fact. Joined to Christ’s death, you were released from the old regime; death dissolves every bond (Romans 7:1–6). Taking up its rules again is a freed slave walking back to pick up his old chains.

Do not handle, taste, touch. A religion of prohibitions, piling up: even the faintest contact banned.

Things that perish. Food is eaten and gone and cannot defile the soul (Mark 7:18–19).

Human precepts. “Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Mark 7:7; Isaiah 29:13). Rules God never gave cannot bind a soul God has freed.

An appearance of wisdom. They look rigorous and holy. “Self-made religion” is ethelothrēskia, a word first found here: worship a man chooses rather than God commands. Self-will dressed as devotion.

No value. They fail at the one thing they promise. Starve the body and the flesh grows fat on pride. Rules can trim behaviour but cannot change a heart, and may even inflame what they forbid (Romans 7:5–8).

Is fasting pointless, then? No. Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matthew 6:16–18); Paul disciplined his body (1 Corinthians 9:27). What Paul condemns is rules imposed as the way to holiness or acceptance.

On a Tuesday. Cutting weeds at ground level makes the garden look tidy for a day; the roots live. Only Christ digs out the root (Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:16). Chapter 3 shows how.

3.title: Set Your Minds on Things Above: The Old and the New
3.overview:
Chapter 2 showed that rules cannot defeat sin. Chapter 3 gives the real cure: union with the risen Christ. Since you have been raised with him, set your heart and mind on things above, where Christ reigns; your life is hidden with him and will appear with him in glory. Therefore put to death the old sins (sexual immorality, greed, which is idolatry) and strip off anger, malice, slander and lies, because you have already put off the old self and put on the new, which God is renewing in his image. In this new humanity race, religion, culture and class no longer divide: Christ is all, and in all.

Instead, as God’s chosen and beloved people, put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience and forgiveness, and above all love. Let Christ’s peace rule, let his word dwell in you richly through teaching and song, and do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks. Finally Christ’s lordship enters the home: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters, each with a duty, and those with power given the harder command.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Set Your Minds on Things Above
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul draws the consequence of union with Christ. Because believers have already been raised with him, their ambitions and thinking should be directed to heaven, where Christ reigns, rather than to the earthly concerns that once ruled them. Their old life has ended and their real life is now kept safe with Christ in God, out of sight for the moment. When Christ appears, that hidden life will be revealed, and they will share his glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hidden Life and the Security of the Believer in Christ

Colossians 3:3 — “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — is one of the New Testament’s most comprehensive statements of the security of the believer. The life of the Christian is not exposed to the attacks of the world, the flesh, or the devil in any ultimate sense; it is hidden, concealed, kept safe in the most secure location possible: with Christ, in God. Reformed theology has always grounded assurance of salvation not in the believer’s performance but in the security of their position: in Christ, kept by God. This is why the Christian can face the world’s hostility and the flesh’s internal rebellion without ultimate despair; the life that matters is in a place nothing can reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that their spiritual security depended on correct navigation of the angelic hierarchy, proper observance of festivals and food laws, and achievement of special spiritual states. Paul says: your life is hidden with Christ in God. There is no spiritual power that can reach it; no ritual failure that can revoke it; no ignorance of esoteric knowledge that can diminish it. Now: The Christian whose sense of security rises and falls with their spiritual performance — who feels secure on days of devotional discipline and insecure on days of failure — needs to hear this: your life is hidden. It is not at risk. It is kept by the one whose power infinitely exceeds every force that would threaten it.

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Raised with Christ, believers must seek the things above, where Christ is seated.

If then. “Since”: the same construction as 2:20. Chapter 2 said rules are powerless against sin. The alternative is not no effort and no direction, but a new direction: not down into severity to the body, but up to the risen Christ. Not asceticism, but aspiration.

Raised with Christ. Already true. United to him (2:12), you share his resurrection now (Ephesians 2:5–6). The false teachers urged climbing through fasting and visions to reach heaven; in Christ you are already there.

Seek. Present tense: keep pursuing. Not mystical detachment, despising job and family, which would be the escapism Paul just condemned. The reorientation of desire and ambition around Christ: “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

Seated at God’s right hand. The place of honour and finished work (Psalm 110:1; Hebrews 1:3). He sat down because the work was done, with the powers beneath his feet (2:15).

For worship. The crucified one is the crowned one, and he is yours, reigning as your advocate (Romans 8:34).

verseByVerse.quote: Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must set their minds on things above, not on earthly things.

Set your minds. Phroneite, as in “have this mind” (Philippians 2:5): the settled bent of thought and valuing. Aim the thoughts upward and the life follows (Romans 8:5–6).

Not on earth. Not the created world as such, but perishable things treated as ultimate, including the sins of v. 5.

What it does not mean. Not becoming so heavenly-minded you are no earthly good, nor despising the body or honest pleasures. Paul will give very down-to-earth instructions in a few verses. You still think about the job, the bills and the garden. The question is what your mind is finally set on, what you interpret everything by.

On a Tuesday. An expatriate does his job and pays his way abroad, but his heart is at home, and that colours everything. “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

verseByVerse.quote: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have died, and their life is hidden with Christ in God.

For. Seek what is above because your life is located there.

You have died. The old self, which lived for the world, died and was buried with Christ (Romans 6:2–6). That is why earthly things are no longer your treasure.

Hidden means safe. Stored in the most secure place in the universe, double-wrapped: your life in Christ, and Christ in God. No sin, devil or death can snatch it (John 10:28–29).

Hidden means concealed. Your true life and glory are not yet on display. Hidden is not lost; it is stored until v. 4.

On a Tuesday. On your worst day, when you feel a failure, your life is still safe, because it hangs on Christ, not on your performance. You may look ordinary, aging, weary, like an acorn that does not yet look like an oak. The glory is real and coming (1 John 3:2).

verseByVerse.quote: When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Christ appears, they will appear with him in glory.

Christ who is your life. Not merely the giver of life, but life itself: its source, substance and centre. Not one good thing among many; the whole of it (Galatians 2:20; Philippians 1:21). The final answer to “Christ plus”.

Appears. Brought out of hiding into view. Now enthroned and unseen; one day revealed to all creation. “When”, not “if”.

With him in glory. Your destiny is tied to his. Hidden with him now; revealed with him then, transformed into his likeness (1 John 3:2; Romans 8:17–18).

The hinge. Future glory is the motive for present holiness: “Put to death therefore …” (v. 5).

A textual note. Manuscripts divide between “your life” and “our life”. Either way, Christ is the life of all believers.

For worship. An heir lives unrecognised in working clothes until the coronation, when he is led out and revealed as the king’s son. That is you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Put to Death, Put Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So they must put to death everything in them that belongs to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desire and greed, which is idolatry. These bring God’s wrath, and they once lived that way. Now they must also get rid of anger, rage, malice, slander and filthy talk, and stop lying to one another, since they have taken off the old self and put on the new, which is being renewed in knowledge after its Creator’s image. In that new humanity the old divisions of race, religion, culture and class no longer count; Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification: Putting to Death What Christ Has Already Condemned

John Owen’s great treatise Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers is the most sustained Reformed treatment of what Paul commands in Colossians 3:5. Owen’s central principle — “be killing sin, or it will be killing you” — reflects Paul’s logic exactly. The mortification Paul calls for is not the ascetic self-punishment that the Colossian false teachers practiced and Paul has just condemned (2:23); it is the Spirit-enabled application of the cross to specific sinful desires, the practical reckoning with what Christ accomplished: these desires belong to the old self that died in Christ; by the Spirit I put them to death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered an ascetic program that promised to deal with the flesh by external denial. Paul says: that program has no value in stopping the flesh’s indulgence (2:23). The real program is mortification — not external prohibition but the internal death-dealing of the Spirit to specific desires. The difference is not severity (asceticism can be more severe than mortification) but source: mortification flows from union with the crucified Christ. Now: The Christian who is fighting sin through willpower and self-discipline alone is using the wrong weapons. Mortification is spiritual warfare: the application of Christ’s death to specific sin patterns, in prayer, by the Spirit, in the community of faith. The fight is real; the weapon is the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must put to death whatever is earthly in them: sexual sin, evil desire and covetousness, which is idolatry.

Therefore. Because you died and were raised with Christ. Become what you are.

Not asceticism. Not rules imposed from outside (2:23), but killing sin from inside, by people already dead and raised with Christ.

Put to death. Nekroō: kill, execute. Not manage or tame. Sin is an enemy, not a pet.

How? You have died with Christ once for all (v. 3), and must put sin to death daily; the finished fact fuels the fight. It is done “by the Spirit” (Romans 8:13): name the sin, refuse it, starve it, flee the temptation, leaning on his power, fighting from favour, not for it. John Owen: “Be killing sin, or it will be killing you.”

From deed to desire. Sexual immorality (porneia, every sexual act outside marriage), impurity (the defiled imagination), passion (ungoverned lust), evil desire (the wrong craving of the heart). Sin runs all the way down, which is why rules can trim the deed but not the desire.

Greed is idolatry. Pleonexia, the craving for more. To covet is to look to created things for the security and worth only God gives (Ephesians 5:5; Matthew 6:24). It exposes the idolatry beneath every sin on the list, and it wears a respectable coat, just wanting a nicer life. “One’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15).

On a Tuesday. Which sin do you tolerate as a pet? Name it to God today, and cut off its supply.

verseByVerse.quote: On account of these the wrath of God is coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of these things the wrath of God is coming.

Why so ruthless? Because these are exactly what God’s judgment is set against.

Wrath. Not bad temper, but the settled, holy opposition of a good God to evil. A judge who felt nothing about injustice would be no good judge (Romans 1:18; 2:5).

Coming. Real, and on its way.

For the believer. Sobriety and relief: this is the wrath that fell on Christ in our place (2:14), from which we are rescued (1 Thessalonians 1:10). All the more reason not to dabble in what cost him so much.

A textual note. Many manuscripts add “upon the sons of disobedience” (KJV), probably from Ephesians 5:6. Some of the earliest lack it; scholars are divided.

verseByVerse.quote: In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They once walked in these ways.

Not that everyone does everything. People outside Christ differ greatly; many are decent and restrained, by God’s common grace. Paul says this was the Colossians’ former road, and that these sins are the native air of life turned from God (1:21).

You too. Even God’s holy people were once there. It keeps believers humble (do not despise those still trapped) and grateful.

Once. That was your old country. You have emigrated; do not move back (1 Corinthians 6:11; Titus 3:3–5).

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to look down on someone caught in these sins, remember: “such were some of you.”

verseByVerse.quote: But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now they must also put away anger, malice, slander and obscene talk.

Put away. Where v. 5 said “kill”, v. 8 says “take off”, like filthy clothes.

How? Not white-knuckled willpower, but putting off paired with putting on (vv. 10, 12): take off anger and put on compassion. Sin is expelled not by a vacuum but by a stronger affection, and it flows from who you already are (v. 9). It is a lifetime’s work by the Spirit, so continued struggle is not proof you are not Christ’s (Ephesians 4:22–24).

The list, from heart to mouth. Anger (orgē): the settled, smouldering grudge. Wrath (thymos): the sudden outburst. Malice: the ill-will beneath both. Slander (blasphēmia): speech that runs a person down. Obscene talk: foul speech. The tongue is the drain through which the heart empties (Matthew 12:34).

Is all anger sinful? No. Jesus looked at the Pharisees “with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart” (Mark 3:5); “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). Anger at real wrong can be righteous. Paul forbids selfish, settled anger that wants to hurt.

Slander or warning? Three tests. Is it true? Is it necessary, for a good end? And why are you saying it: in love, to someone who can act, or with relish behind a back?

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having put off the old self and put on the new, they must not lie to one another.

Do not lie. Not only bald untruths, but half-truths, spin, flattery and broken promises. “To one another”: lying poisons the trust that holds the church together. The devil is the father of lies (John 8:44).

Already done. “Put off” and “put on” are completed acts. The old self, the whole person you were in Adam, was crucified with Christ at conversion (Romans 6:6). Daily putting away of his leftover habits lives out a removal already done.

Being renewed. The tense changes to continuous and passive: God is renewing the new self day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16; Romans 12:2). Already, and not yet: the decisive change is done; the transformation goes on.

In knowledge. Not the false teachers’ secret knowledge, but knowing God truly in Christ (2:3), reversing the darkened mind of Romans 1:21.

After the image. Back to Genesis 1:26–27: the image defaced by the fall is being restored in Christ, the image of God (1:15; Romans 8:29). A master restorer cleaning a painted-over portrait, stroke by stroke.

Is lying ever right? Some hold that deceiving would-be murderers is not the lying Scripture forbids, since God dealt well with the midwives (Exodus 1:20). Others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold every lie a sin, though God may honour the faith behind it. The second is more likely, but such cases are rare. The command concerns trust among believers.

On a Tuesday. Be someone whose word can always be relied on, even in small things: the excuse, the expense claim, the CV.

verseByVerse.quote: Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the new humanity distinctions of race, religion, culture and class are nothing; Christ is all and in all.

The new self is corporate. Christ is forming a new humanity, and in it the old walls do not stand.

Every division. Race (Greek and Jew, the deepest divide); religion (circumcised and uncircumcised); culture (a “barbarian” was anyone whose speech sounded like babble to Greeks; Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were the byword for the wildest of all); class (slave and free).

Dethroned, not erased. A Jew is still a Jew, a slave still a slave. But none of it decides worth, standing before God, or place in the family (Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 2:14–16).

Christ is all. In place of labels that rank and divide, one defining reality.

In all. The same Christ lives in every believer, polished or rough, and that makes them one.

On a Tuesday. Is there a kind of person you would rather not sit next to in church? Go and sit there.
verseByVerse.note: Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were thought of as the most uncivilised of barbarians.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God’s chosen people, holy and loved, they are to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, bearing with and forgiving one another as the Lord forgave them, and above all with love, which binds everything together. Christ’s peace is to rule in their hearts, and they should be thankful. The word of Christ is to dwell richly among them as they teach and admonish one another and sing to God with gratitude. Whatever they do, in word or deed, they are to do it in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to the Father through him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Virtues of the New Self as the Character of Christ

The list of virtues in Colossians 3:12–15 is nothing less than a portrait of Christ himself: compassionate, kind, humble, meek, patient, forgiving, loving, peaceful. Reformed theology understands sanctification as progressive conformity to the image of Christ (Rom 8:29); the virtues Paul commands here are the specific contours of that image. They are not generated by the believer through moral effort; they are produced by the Spirit as the fruit of genuine union with Christ (compare the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23). The community that puts on these virtues is the community that is becoming what it already is in Christ: holy and beloved.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian community, like every early Christian community, was a mixture of people from very different backgrounds — Jewish, Greek, slave, free — with very different habits of relating and conflicting. The virtues Paul commands were counter-cultural in every direction: humility was scorned by Graeco-Roman aristocratic culture; forgiveness was a novelty in a world organized around honour and revenge. Now: The church remains the most diverse social reality in the world, and the virtues Paul commands remain equally counter-cultural. The church that is genuinely putting on compassion, kindness, humility, and forbearance will look radically different from any other community the world contains, because these virtues are the character of the one who was raised for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As God’s chosen and beloved people, they must put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, forgiveness and above all love.

Get dressed. Not only stopping the bad, but clothing yourself with the good, deliberately and daily, often before the feeling arrives.

Identity first. Chosen (Ephesians 1:4), holy, beloved (sharing the Son’s belovedness, 1:13). You do not put these on to become loved, but because you are. The beloved can afford to love.

Compassion and kindness. Pity moved by another’s pain, turned into action (Romans 2:4).

Humility. The word the false teachers twisted (2:18), here the real thing: a right estimate of yourself as a sinner saved by grace (Philippians 2:3). Not self-hatred, which is self-absorption with a long face. Not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less.

Meekness. Used of a horse broken in: power under control. Jesus was “gentle and lowly” (Matthew 11:29) and cleansed the temple.

Bearing with one another. Putting up with rough edges: the brother who talks too long, the sister always late. Families do it round the breakfast table.

As the Lord forgave you. Freely, fully, before you asked (Romans 5:8–10).

Forgive before they apologise? The forgiving heart, releasing bitterness, always and at once (Mark 11:25). Full reconciliation when the other repents (Luke 17:3); restoration takes two.

After abuse? Forgiving means letting go of revenge and handing the wrong to God. It does not mean trusting a dangerous person, resuming contact, keeping abuse secret, or giving up the protection of the law (Romans 13:4). Reconciliation needs repentance and changed behaviour; safety comes first.

Love above all. Not mainly feeling, but a settled will to seek another’s good at cost (1 Corinthians 13). The syndesmos, the ligament (2:19), that ties every grace and the whole body together.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “as Christ forgave you” (KJV), others “as God”. “The Lord” is best attested.

verseByVerse.quote: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The peace of Christ must rule in their hearts, and they must be thankful.

The peace of Christ. The peace he made by the cross (1:20): first with God, then the calm he gives (John 14:27), then peace between his people.

Rule. Brabeuetō, the umpire’s word. When torn, anxious, or pulled two ways in a decision, let his peace make the call. Do not let anger, fear or self-will referee your heart.

One body. Not merely private calm, but the bond that keeps the church one (v. 11).

Be thankful. The first of three calls to thanks in three verses. The thankful heart is the peaceful heart; gratitude crowds out grievance (Philippians 4:6–7).

A textual note. Later manuscripts read “the peace of God” (KJV). “Of Christ” is earlier.

On a Tuesday. Facing a decision? Ask which option you could take with Christ’s peace, and which would need you to override it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of Christ must dwell in them richly as they teach one another and sing to God.

The word of Christ. The gospel about him (1:5), and all Scripture that testifies to him, against “philosophy and empty deceit” (2:8).

Dwell richly. A resident, not a guest, furnishing every room. By reading, hearing, pondering and memorising. This is how the mind is renewed (v. 10).

Teaching and admonishing one another. Truth imparted and wrong warned against, by every member, not only official teachers, with wisdom to know what the moment needs.

Psalms, hymns, spiritual songs. Probably the full range of sung worship: the Psalter, songs of praise like 1:15–20, Spirit-prompted songs. Sung truth lodges in the heart as nothing else does (Ephesians 5:19).

Only psalms? Those who hold exclusive psalmody note all three words appear in the titles of the Greek Psalter. But the New Testament itself contains songs about Christ (Philippians 2:6–11; 1 Timothy 3:16). The more likely reading is that the church may sing psalms and new songs faithful to Scripture.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “the word of God” or “of the Lord”. “Of Christ” is best attested.

On a Tuesday. Learn one psalm or hymn by heart this month. It will teach you when nothing else can.

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever they do, in word or deed, must be done in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks.

Whatever. Nothing left out: word and deed, the whole of life. No secular corner.

In the name. As his representative: on his behalf, under his authority, for his honour, by his help. It consecrates the ordinary and constrains the sinful; you cannot do in his name what dishonours it.

Not a fence of rules. Against 2:20–23, Christ’s lordship reaches every act from the inside (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Through him. The third call to thanks. Thanks reach the Father through Christ, the one Mediator: no angels needed (Ephesians 5:20).

On a Tuesday. Before your next task, however dull, say: “Lord Jesus, I do this for you.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul applies this to the household, the basic unit of ancient society. Wives are to submit to their husbands as fitting in the Lord, and husbands are to love their wives and not be harsh with them. Children are to obey their parents, which pleases the Lord, and fathers are not to provoke their children and discourage them. Slaves are to obey their earthly masters sincerely, not to win favour, but working wholeheartedly as for the Lord, from whom they will receive the inheritance; wrongdoers will be repaid without favouritism. Masters must treat their slaves justly and fairly, knowing they too have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lordship of Christ in the Household: Sacred and Ordinary

The household code illustrates one of Reformed theology’s most important convictions: there is no sacred-secular divide. The lordship of Christ claimed in the great hymn of chapter 1 arrives in chapter 3 at the level of household management, parenting, and the workplace. Abraham Kuyper’s “every square inch” is not abstract theology; it is the practical implication of “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17). The Christian who is an excellent spouse, a patient parent, and an honest worker is doing theology in the most concrete possible form.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Graeco-Roman household was organized around the absolute authority of the paterfamilias — husband, father, master. Over children and slaves his authority was close to absolute in law. Paul does not abolish this structure but fills it with a different spirit: love, not domination; encouragement, not provocation; justice, not exploitation. The counterpart to every command of submission is a command of love and care that was genuinely counter-cultural. Now: The application of these principles in contemporary household and work relationships continues to produce the same counter-cultural witness: the Christian employee who works with integrity “as to the Lord” even when unsupervised; the Christian employer who treats workers with justice and fairness; the Christian parent who encourages rather than exasperates. Each is a small enactment of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wives are to submit to their husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

Christ in the home. After v. 17, the lordship of Christ enters the household. Ancient household codes laid duties on the lesser party; Paul addresses both, and gives the stronger the harder command.

Submit. Hypotassō, middle voice: to arrange oneself under, freely. Not seized by the husband. Respect, support and trust; and in a genuine deadlock, after prayer and honest discussion, trusting his lead.

Your own husbands. One marriage, not women under men in general.

What it does not mean. Not inferiority: she is a co-heir of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7; Galatians 3:28); the Son is equal to the Father yet does his will. Not slavish obedience: children and slaves are told to “obey” (vv. 20, 22), wives to “submit”. Not silence: she is a strong helper (Genesis 2:18) who speaks and may disagree. Not obeying into sin (Acts 5:29). Never submission to abuse: the next verse forbids harshness, and the church must protect, not preach “submit”.

Views. Egalitarian Christians read this in light of mutual submission (Ephesians 5:21) and Galatians 3:28, and see the household codes as tied to culture. But Paul grounds headship in Christ and the church, not culture (Ephesians 5:23–25), and gives husbands a different command. The more likely reading is equal worth with different callings.

In the Lord. It dignifies her submission as devotion to Christ, roots it in him, and limits it: it can never dishonour the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Most decisions in a healthy marriage are simply made together. Speak well of your husband, and back him rather than undercut him (Ephesians 5:33; 1 Peter 3:5–6).

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Husbands must love their wives and never be harsh with them.

Love. Agapē: the self-giving love of the will. The measure: “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Headship by sacrifice, not domination.

The harder command. Ancient codes told husbands almost nothing. Paul lays the heavier duty on the man.

What it looks like. Her good above his comfort; constant, not rising and falling with feelings; nourishing and cherishing (Ephesians 5:28–29); serving in small, unglamorous ways, as the Lord washed feet (John 13:5).

Do not be harsh. From pikros, bitter: do not grow sharp or sour. The husband’s typical temptation: strength curdling into domination, small resentments hardening. The cutting tone, sarcasm, endless criticism, silence as a weapon. Often the man pleasant with everyone else who saves his harshness for his wife.

The cure. The compassion, meekness and patience of v. 12, and ready forgiveness (v. 13). A wife was given to be loved as Christ loves, not to be a target (1 Peter 3:7).

On a Tuesday. Husbands: do one unasked, unglamorous thing for your wife today, and speak to her as gently as you speak to your colleagues.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children must obey their parents, for this pleases the Lord.

Spoken to children. They are real members of the church, able to hear and answer God’s word.

Obey. To listen and do. For a young child, glad, prompt obedience: the nursery of discipleship. For a teenager, honour and trust: keeping household rules, receiving correction. For a grown child, obedience gives way to lifelong honour and care (Ephesians 6:2; 1 Timothy 5:4, 8).

In everything. Wide but not absolute: “obey your parents in the Lord” (Ephesians 6:1). Never into sin (Acts 5:29). That exception is rare.

Pleases the Lord. The eternal Son spent thirty years in a carpenter’s home and “was submissive” to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51). He came “not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). An obedient child bears the family likeness of the obedient Son.

For children. When you obey, you bring joy to God’s heart, not to win his love but because you belong to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers must not provoke their children, lest they lose heart.

Provoke. To irritate, exasperate. Ephesians 6:4 adds: “but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.” The one with power gets the restraining word.

How fathers provoke. Harshness, never-satisfied criticism, favouritism, punishing in temper, impossible expectations, domineering control, hypocrisy, cold neglect.

By age. A young child: impatience over spilled cups, anger out of proportion, rules that change with mood. The good way: gentleness, clear boundaries held warmly, generous praise. A school child: constant criticism, comparison with siblings, praise that never comes. The good way: specific praise, interest in his world, fair discipline explained. A teenager: control that never loosens, endless lectures, “because I said so”. The good way: trust growing with responsibility, listening, choosing battles, owning your own faults. A grown child: still dictating. The good way: bless rather than control.

Discouraged. A bruised little heart; a child who gives up trying (“I’ll never be good enough for him”); a teen in rebellion or joyless withdrawal.

The pattern. Father as God fathers: “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him” (Psalm 103:13). Firm yet tender (Hebrews 12:7–11).

On a Tuesday. Fathers: catch your child doing something right today, and say so.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Slaves are to serve sincerely as for the Lord, who will reward and judge without partiality.

Roman slavery. A large share of the population. Not the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries: people became slaves by war, birth or debt; many were educated, held money and could be freed. Harsh and varied. Onesimus, a runaway slave, carried this letter home (4:9; Philemon).

Not blessing the system. Paul urges freedom where possible (1 Corinthians 7:21) and makes master and slave brothers (Philemon 16). He teaches how to live for Christ inside a system the gospel would dissolve. The how-to-work carries across to any job; the conditions do not.

Earthly masters. Literally “masters according to the flesh”: only on the passing level. You have a greater Master.

Eye-service. A word Paul may have coined: working only while watched. Looking busy when the manager passes, gaming the metrics.

Heartily. “From the soul”, as for the Lord. A mean master cannot rob a swept floor of its glory.

The inheritance. Under Roman law a slave could not inherit. Paul promises the inheritance of God’s people (1:12). Not wages earned, but a son’s portion, God crowning service his grace enabled.

No partiality. A warning both ways: the slave cannot get away with spiteful work, and the master who wrongs him will not escape (Romans 2:11).

On a Tuesday. The cleaner mopping an empty corridor, the clerk filling the same forms, the carer washing a body no one else will touch: done for the Lord, it is laid in the hands of the King. Your foreman may never say thank you. The Lord forgets nothing (1 Corinthians 15:58).
verseByVerse.note: One of the slaves in the church was Onesimus, returning to his master in Colossae with this letter.
