You are serving the Lord Christ.<sup>25</sup>For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.

4.title: Devoted to Prayer: Wisdom, Words, and the Gospel Network
4.overview:
The household code ends with a word to masters: treat your slaves justly and fairly, because you have a Master in heaven. Then Paul turns outward. Keep praying, alert and thankful, and pray for him: not that his prison door would open, but a door for the gospel, and that he would speak it clearly. Live wisely towards outsiders, seizing every opportunity, with speech that is gracious and seasoned with salt.

The letter closes with a page of names that shows the gospel in human form: Tychicus the courier, Onesimus the runaway slave now called a faithful brother, Mark the restored deserter, Epaphras wrestling in prayer, Luke the doctor, Demas who would later leave, Nympha and the church in her house, and Archippus, charged to finish his ministry. Paul signs with his chained hand: “Remember my chains. Grace be with you.”

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Masters must treat their slaves justly and fairly, for they too have a Master in heaven.

The power they held. A Roman master could command, punish, sell and in law even kill his slaves. Aristotle called a slave “a living tool”. Duties ran one way. Paul turns and lays a duty on the master.

Justly and fairly. “Justly”: what is right and due, discipline by principle, not mood. “Fairly”: isotēs, equity, with a hint that this slave is now your brother (Philemon 16). Far beyond what Roman law asked.

A Master. Kyrioi are told they have a Kyrios. The man at the top of the earthly ladder is himself a servant, and will answer to the Lord with whom there is no partiality (3:25; Ephesians 6:9). Master and slave kneel side by side at one throne.

Today. The bridge is the employer. The old temptation survives: to see people as “human resources”, valued only for output.

On a Tuesday. Bosses and managers: a fair wage, contracts kept, safe conditions, no favouritism, and the same dignity for the night cleaner and the senior partner. The Christian in authority should be the most just employer in town (Leviticus 25:43).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They are to keep on praying, alert and thankful, and to pray for Paul too, that God will open a door for the message of Christ, for which he is in chains, and that he will make it clear as he should. They should act wisely towards outsiders, making the most of every opportunity, and their conversation should always be gracious and well seasoned, so that they know how to answer each person.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer as Steadfast Engagement, Not Occasional Request

Paul’s instruction to “continue steadfastly in prayer” (proskartereite) reflects the Reformed conviction that prayer is not an emergency resort but the fundamental posture of the creature before the Creator. The same verb is used in Acts 1:14 of the disciples’ prayer in the upper room and in Acts 2:42 of the early church’s corporate life. Steadfast prayer is the mark of a community that has genuinely reckoned with its dependence on God and genuinely believes that prayer moves the hands that move the world.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul, in prison, could not personally open the doors for the gospel’s advance. He could pray — and he could enlist the Colossians to pray with him. The prayer for open doors is the prayer of the person who has surrendered control of the gospel’s advance to the one who actually controls it. Now: The church that wants to reach the lost but neglects corporate prayer has misunderstood the mechanism by which God works. Open doors are God’s to give; prayer is the community’s engagement with the God who gives them.

verseByVerse.quote: Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must keep on praying, watchful and thankful.

Continue steadfastly. Proskartereite: to persevere doggedly, as the first church “devoted themselves” to prayer (Acts 2:42; compare 1:14). That Paul must command it shows it is hard: prayer is hidden work, answers tarry, the flesh is weak, and the enemy would rather we did anything else. Jesus told the persistent widow’s parable “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1).

Watchful. The sentry who dare not doze. The memory of Gethsemane: “Watch and pray” (Matthew 26:41). Pray awake, mind present; with eyes open to what needs prayer and for God’s answer. Prayer’s great enemy is not hostility but drowsiness.

With thanksgiving. Again (1:3, 12; 2:7; 3:15–17). It keeps prayer from becoming a list of demands, and the grateful pray-er is the persevering one (Philippians 4:6).

On a Tuesday. Do not measure your prayer by how it feels. Simply do not stop. Begin today’s prayer with three specific thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison— that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They should pray for an open door for the word, and for Paul to make the mystery of Christ clear.

Pray for us. The apostle who saw the risen Christ asks a small church he has never met to pray for him. No one outgrows the need, and the humblest believer’s prayers truly count (Romans 15:30; Ephesians 6:19).

A door for the word. Paul’s picture for opportunity (1 Corinthians 16:9; 2 Corinthians 2:12). God opens it. And a man in chains asks not for the prison door but for the gospel’s door: “the word of God is not bound” (2 Timothy 2:9).

The mystery of Christ. The once-hidden secret, now open, who is a Person (1:26–27; 2:2).

On account of which I am in prison. No complaint against Rome, his accusers or God. Not Caesar’s prisoner but “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 3:1). “What has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel” (Philippians 1:12).

Make it clear. Even the greatest preacher asks prayer to speak plainly. An open door is wasted without a clear message.

On a Tuesday. What do you do with your own prisons: the unjust treatment, the shut door? Pray for your preacher’s clarity on Sunday, and for your own when you next explain your hope.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must walk wisely towards outsiders, making the best use of time.

From his witness to theirs. Pray for the gospel’s advance, and live so as to advance it.

Outsiders. Non-Christians around them. The world reads the gospel first in the lives of those who profess it.

Walk in wisdom. With the skill and tact of the wisdom hidden in Christ (2:3): integrity in business, kindness, a blameless life that disarms criticism (1 Peter 2:12), knowing when to speak and when to stay quiet.

Two ditches. Compromise, blending into the world; and harsh superiority, the sour believer the world rightly recoils from. The only offence we should give is the gospel’s.

Buying up the time. Kairos, the opportune moment, not the clock. A merchant snapping up a bargain before it goes (Ephesians 5:16).

On a Tuesday. The colleague in a hard season, the unexpected question about your hope: that window may not open again. Buy it up.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their speech must always be gracious and seasoned with salt, ready to answer everyone.

Always. All your talk, not only religious talk.

Gracious. Kind, winsome, and giving grace to the hearer (Ephesians 4:29), like the “gracious words” of Jesus (Luke 4:22).

Seasoned with salt. Salt gave food flavour and kept it from spoiling. Speech with savour and substance, wholesome, not coarse. Not today’s “salty”, meaning crude.

Both together. Gracious without salt is kind but bland. Salted without grace is clever but cruel. Be kind and interesting, truthful and winsome.

Each person. Not one canned formula but an answer fitted to this person’s question. “Always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15).

Soil and fruit. Winsome everyday speech draws the questions; harsh or insipid talk shuts them down (Proverbs 15:23).

On a Tuesday. Answer the next hostile remark with unexpected kindness rather than defensiveness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul closes with news and greetings that show the network of people behind his mission. Tychicus will bring the letter and his news, together with Onesimus, the runaway slave now a faithful brother. Aristarchus, Mark (Barnabas’s cousin), and Jesus called Justus send greetings, the only Jewish believers working with him, and a comfort to him. Epaphras, their own founder, wrestles in prayer for them and for Laodicea and Hierapolis. Luke the doctor and Demas greet them. Paul asks them to greet the church in Nympha’s house, to exchange letters with Laodicea, and to tell Archippus to complete his ministry. He signs the greeting in his own hand: remember my chains; grace be with you.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Community of the Gospel as the Body of Christ

The list of names at the end of Colossians is the practical expression of the ecclesiology of 1:18: Christ is the head of the body, the church. The body is not an abstract entity; it is Tychicus and Onesimus and Luke and Nympha. The community of grace is always concrete, always named, always embodied in particular people with particular histories, gifts, and needs. Reformed ecclesiology has always insisted on the visible, particular, local church as the primary form of the body of Christ: not an ideal church somewhere, but this church, these people, this place, this time.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Onesimus is the most striking name on the list. The runaway slave, the subject of the letter to Philemon, is now a “faithful and beloved brother” being commended to the Colossians. The gospel has done exactly what Paul said it would do in 3:11: it has abolished the slave/free distinction as a defining category. Onesimus and Philemon are brothers; Onesimus and the Colossians are family. Now: The community of the gospel is always the community of the surprising, the reconciled, the transformed. The people who would never have been in the same room together are gathered at the same table because Christ is all, and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tychicus will bring news and encouragement.

Do not skim the names. This roll-call is a photograph of the gospel at work: “beloved brother”, “faithful minister”, “fellow servant”, “fellow prisoner”. Family, not colleagues.

Tychicus. The courier, from the province of Asia (Acts 20:4), who carried this letter and Ephesians on the same journey (Ephesians 6:21–22), with Onesimus beside him.

Two jobs. To give news of Paul, and to encourage their hearts (the verb of 2:2). The word arrived in the hands of a man commissioned to love the people he was sent to. It has never travelled another way.

No authority. Not sent to inspect or correct a church flirting with error, but to reassure. Sometimes the most useful thing you can carry into a troubled congregation is your steady presence.

A textual note. Manuscripts divide between “that you may know how we are” (ESV) and “that he may know how you are” (KJV). The words differ by a letter or two. The ESV reading fits the next verse better.

On a Tuesday. Visit a struggling believer this week with no agenda but encouragement.

verseByVerse.quote: and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Onesimus, once a runaway slave, comes as a faithful and beloved brother.

Who he was. The runaway slave of Philemon, a Colossian Christian. A runaway was a criminal in Roman law, liable to branding, flogging or worse. He is walking back into the town he fled.

The same titles. Not “whom I am returning to his master”. “Our faithful and beloved brother”: the very words just used of Tychicus, a free man and apostolic delegate.

One of you. Not tolerated: belonging, with the same standing as the man who owns him. Read aloud in the room where Philemon sat.

3:11 walking through the door. Paul does not stage a revolt against Rome’s slave system. He does something slower and more corrosive to it: he puts a runaway and a delegate side by side, gives them one name, and calls them brothers.

For anyone with a past. Onesimus had a record and everyone knew it. The gospel does not pretend a history away, and refuses to let it be a man’s name.
verseByVerse.note: Onesimus was the runaway slave of Philemon, a member of the church at Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aristarchus, Mark and Jesus Justus, Paul’s Jewish fellow workers, send greetings.

Aristarchus. From Thessalonica (Acts 20:4); seized by the mob at Ephesus (Acts 19:29); on the voyage that ended in shipwreck (Acts 27:2). “Fellow prisoner” is literally “fellow prisoner of war”, perhaps sharing custody voluntarily.

Mark. The wound healing. He deserted the first missionary journey (Acts 13:13), and Paul refused to take him again, splitting from Barnabas (Acts 15:37–39). Now Paul writes ahead to ensure a welcome. Later: “Get Mark … for he is very useful to me for ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). Tradition holds he wrote the second Gospel. Grace restores those who fail, and those they failed.

Jesus called Justus. A common Jewish name, the Greek form of Joshua, with a Roman name added. Not the Lord.

The only Jews. A quiet ache from the man who wished himself accursed for his kinsmen (Romans 9:3).

A comfort. Parēgoria, only here in the New Testament: a medical word, a soothing that eases pain.

The kingdom of God. Already here, since God “has transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (1:13), and not yet consummated until Christ returns. We live in it and labour for it (Romans 14:17; Acts 28:31).

On a Tuesday. Is there someone who once let you down whom you should now welcome back?
verseByVerse.note: Mark had once left Paul, causing a split with Barnabas; he is now restored.

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras labours in prayer for them, that they may stand mature and fully assured.

The founder. He brought them the gospel (1:7), and his report prompted the letter.

Struggling. Agōnizomenos, the wrestler’s word, as of Paul’s labour (1:29). Not mentioning Colossae in his devotions: wrestling. If prayer is combat, “all I can do is pray” has misunderstood which activity is strenuous.

The whole letter in one petition. Stand: not shifted off Christ (2:6–7). Mature: teleioi, the goal of 1:28; not an advanced inner circle, but the growing-up of people already filled (2:10). Fully assured: carried to settled conviction. In all the will of God: not esoteric secrets.

A textual note. Later manuscripts read “complete” (KJV) instead of “fully assured”, and “great zeal” instead of “worked hard” in v. 13. The meaning is close.

Three towns. Colossae, Laodicea (wealthy banking centre) and Hierapolis (famous hot springs), within a dozen miles in the Lycus valley. Epaphras evangelised them all, and Paul vouches for him.

On a Tuesday. Most of our praying is for circumstances to improve. Pray this week for the maturity and assurance of the people you love.
verseByVerse.note: Hierapolis lay across the valley from Laodicea.

verseByVerse.quote: Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke the beloved physician and Demas send greetings.

Luke. Author of the third Gospel and Acts; only here are we told his trade. It fits his careful research (Luke 1:3) and his interest in illness. The “we” passages of Acts show him travelling with Paul.

A physician at hand. Paul had a lasting affliction (2 Corinthians 12:7; Galatians 4:13–14), five floggings, a stoning, three shipwrecks. Providence placed a doctor beside him. At the end: “Luke alone is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). God works through ordinary means; using medicine is no lack of faith.

Demas. Three words, no title. Years later: “Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me” (2 Timothy 4:10). Not heresy or scandal, but the respectable pull of a quieter life. That is how most people leave: not with a repudiation, but with a drift.

Did he lose his salvation? Scripture does not tell us his end. If he never returned, he showed he had never truly belonged (1 John 2:19); he may have returned.

Side by side. The man who stayed and the man who did not, both in the room, indistinguishable that day.

On a Tuesday. Not all who begin well finish well. Be watchful, not smug, and pray that you may stand.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, the author of Luke and Acts, was a doctor. Demas later deserted Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets the believers at Laodicea and Nympha’s house church.

Nympha. A woman with means, who used them: a congregation met in her home. For two centuries there were no church buildings; homes had to be large enough and their owners willing to attract official attention. Lydia (Acts 16:15), Priscilla (1 Corinthians 16:19) and Mary the mother of Mark (Acts 12:12) did the same.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “Nymphas” (a man) and “his house” (KJV); others “their house”. The feminine is better supported; a later scribe may have found a woman host surprising.

The shape of a church. A room, not a hall; a group small enough to eat together. Bearing with one another (3:13) meant people who could not avoid each other’s faults.

Laodicea. Ten miles off, rich, famous for black wool and eye-salve. Paul knits the valley’s churches together.

A shadow. A generation later Christ wrote to this church: “you say, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing, not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17). Churches greeted warmly by an apostle can still drift.

On a Tuesday. Could your home host a small group or a meal for newcomers?
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes.

verseByVerse.quote: And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letters are to be read in both churches.

Read among you. Aloud, to the gathered church. Few owned books, so Scripture came through the ears in a room full of people. Paul wrote for the ear.

Public documents. From the beginning, for the whole people of God. Churches swapped, copied and read one another’s letters: the first stirring of the New Testament collection.

The letter from Laodicea. We do not know. Perhaps lost; Paul wrote at least one other letter to Corinth we do not have (1 Corinthians 5:9). Perhaps the circular we call Ephesians, reaching Laodicea first. A later forgery under that name was rightly rejected.

What it does not mean. Not a gap in the Bible. The canon is not everything the apostles wrote, but what God caused to be kept for his church.

On a Tuesday. Read a whole letter of Paul aloud in one sitting. It was written to be heard.
verseByVerse.note: The letter from Laodicea has not survived; some think it may be the letter we know as Ephesians.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Archippus must fulfil the ministry he has received in the Lord.

Archippus. Named with Philemon and Apphia as “our fellow soldier” (Philemon 1–2), probably of that household, perhaps their son. Something had stalled; no rebuke, but the charge would not be needed if all were well.

Public. The whole church is to say it to him. A church holds its members to what they have taken on; a man gone quiet is better served by people who expect something of him than by everyone looking away.

Received. A trust handed to him, not a career chosen. You may resign a job you selected; a trust is someone else’s property in your hands.

Fulfil. Fill it full, carry it through to the end.

A possible link. Philemon’s household was exactly where Onesimus was returning (v. 9), the home about to be tested hardest. Paul does not join the threads, and we should not force them.

On a Tuesday. The only person in the list given a charge is an ordinary Christian whose ministry we cannot even identify. You have been given something too. Finish it.
verseByVerse.note: Archippus was probably a member of Philemon’s household.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul signs with his own hand: remember my chains; grace be with you.

My own hand. Paul dictated (Tertius penned Romans, Romans 16:22) and signed the close himself: authentication against forgeries (2 Thessalonians 3:17), and affection.

Remember my chains. Roman custody meant a wrist chained to a guard. The iron scraped as he wrote. The letter that says Christ is the image of God, in whom all things hold together, was written in irons.

Not self-pity. No complaint in the whole letter. A request for prayer (v. 3), and an argument: nobody wears irons for a lie. Teachers who risked nothing offered a more sophisticated religion; the gospel came from a man paying for it in metal.

Grace. The first word answers the last (1:2). To a church told it could climb to God by rules, festivals, visions and severity, the final word is not effort, secret knowledge or a higher tier, but grace.

A textual note. Many manuscripts add “Amen”.

For worship. From grace, to grace, all the way home.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then signed the greeting himself.
